q: Why is proxy.ts not enough to protect data?
It only covers the routes its matcher lists and can be bypassed or misconfigured; Server Actions and new routes need their own checks next to the data.
What does the server-only import protect against?
It makes the build fail if code that handles secrets or auth is imported into a client bundle.

next-caching.md:
## Why it exists
Rendering on every request is slow and expensive, and serving stale data forever is wrong. **Caching** balances the two, and Next.js changed its model in version 16: the older implicit caching of the App Router was replaced by an explicit, opt-in model called **Cache Components**.

{{dg:0}}

## How it works
Turn it on in config, then mark what is cacheable with the `'use cache'` directive. Anything not marked runs at request time. Next.js builds a static shell from the cached and static parts and streams the dynamic parts into it. This combination is called **Partial Pre-Rendering (PPR)**.
```ts
// next.config.ts
import type { NextConfig } from 'next'

const nextConfig: NextConfig = { cacheComponents: true }
export default nextConfig
```

## Worked example
```tsx
// lib/posts.ts
import { cacheLife, cacheTag } from 'next/cache'

export async function getPosts() {
  'use cache'
  cacheTag('posts')        // a label you can invalidate later
  cacheLife('hours')       // how long it may be served before refreshing
  return db.posts.findMany()
}
```
```ts
// app/posts/actions.ts
'use server'
import { updateTag } from 'next/cache'

export async function createPost(formData: FormData) {
  await db.posts.create({ data: { title: String(formData.get('title')) } })
  updateTag('posts')       // the next read sees fresh data immediately
}
```
`updateTag` expires the tag right away, which suits Server Actions where a user must see their own change. `revalidateTag` marks it stale and refreshes in the background (stale-while-revalidate). Check the exact signature in the docs for your installed version.

## What changed from older versions
| Topic | Next.js 14 and 15 App Router | Next.js 16 with Cache Components |
|---|---|---|
| Default | Fetches and routes cached implicitly in many cases | Nothing is cached unless you opt in |
| How to cache | fetch options and route segment config | `'use cache'` on a page, component or function |
| Static plus dynamic | A page was one or the other | Static shell plus streamed dynamic parts (PPR) |
| Request interception | `middleware.ts` | `proxy.ts`, running on the Node.js runtime |

## In real products
- Marketing and docs pages: cache with a long `cacheLife` and invalidate by tag when the CMS publishes, using a webhook.
- Product pages: cache the catalog data and stream per-user price or stock inside a Suspense boundary.
- Dashboards: never put user-specific data in a shared cache, or one user's data can reach another.

> [!pitfall] Request-time APIs such as cookies() and headers() cannot be read inside a cached scope. Read them outside and pass the values in as arguments, which also become part of the cache key.
> [!pitfall] Upgrading from Next.js 14 or 15 changes caching defaults. Re-test pages that relied on implicit caching instead of assuming they behave the same.
> [!tip] Add a cacheTag to everything you cache. Invalidating by tag is far easier than tracking down paths.
q: What is the main change to caching in Next.js 16?
Caching is explicit and opt-in through 'use cache' with Cache Components, instead of implicit by default.
When would you choose updateTag over revalidateTag?
In a Server Action where the user must immediately see their own change; updateTag expires the cache right away.

q: What does the 'use client' directive actually do?
It marks a module boundary: that file and everything it imports are bundled for the browser and can use state and browser APIs.
Why are Server Actions a security concern?
They are reachable as HTTP endpoints, so each one must check authentication and validate input itself.
